name: Human Development
description: An evidence-based survey of physical, cognitive, language, and socioemotional development from prenatal development through middle childhood, integrating Piaget, Erikson, Vygotsky, attachment research, and contextual influences.

modules.title: Theories of Development
modules.titleZh: 发展理论（皮亚杰、埃里克森、维果茨基）
modules.objectives: Compare Piaget's cognitive stages, Erikson's psychosocial stages, and Vygotsky's sociocultural theory; evaluate each theory's contributions and limitations. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 1.3 — major developmental theories, including Erikson, Piaget, and Vygotsky.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 1: Theories of Development lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Submit: a three-column comparison chart and a 250-word evidence-based conclusion. Include: Piaget, Erikson, and Vygotsky compared by primary question, mechanism of development, role of social context, age or stage assumptions, educational implication, one contribution, and one limitation; cite the assigned OpenStax section. Apply the theories to this fictional example: a teacher first models fraction tiles, then gives hints while a 10-year-old solves a new fraction problem, and gradually removes help as the student succeeds. Explain which theory best fits the example and what the other two still contribute. Evaluation: all three theories are represented accurately, comparisons use source evidence, and the conclusion acknowledges that the theories address partly different questions.

modules.title: Prenatal Development & Birth
modules.objectives: Describe the three stages of prenatal development (germinal, embryonic, fetal), identify teratogens and their critical periods, and explain the birth process and its psychological dimensions.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 2.3 — prenatal stages, teratogens, timing, dose, susceptibility, and context.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 2: Prenatal Development & Birth lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 350-word evidence table and analysis of one teratogen from the assigned source. Include: route of exposure, timing and dose considerations, possible outcomes stated as risks rather than certainties, at least two qualified citations, and one paragraph explaining why exposure does not determine one inevitable outcome. Evaluation: the evidence distinguishes association, mechanism, and uncertainty; uses current qualified sources; and avoids diagnosing an individual pregnancy.

modules.title: Infancy: Physical & Cognitive Development
modules.titleZh: 婴儿期：身体与认知发展
modules.objectives: Describe major physical milestones of infancy, explain the development of sensory and motor abilities, and apply Piaget's sensorimotor stage including object permanence.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e 9.3 — infancy, sensorimotor development, milestones, and the limits of stage-based age ranges.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 3: Infancy: Physical & Cognitive Development lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 3.4 — habituation, dishabituation, infant cognition, memory, and limits of interpreting infant responses; apply it to the fictional Ari case.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 300-word developmental analysis of this fictional case: at 6 months Ari tracks a moving toy and grasps it; at 9 months Ari searches after a toy is partly hidden; at 13 months Ari retrieves a toy hidden under a cloth after a short delay; motor skills and responses vary across situations. Include: five evidence-based behavior-to-concept links, relevant sensorimotor ideas or milestones, and two limits of interpreting one short case. Evaluation: every interpretation cites a stated behavior, uses age ranges as approximate, and avoids diagnosis.

modules.title: Infancy: Social & Emotional Development
modules.titleZh: 婴儿期：社会与情绪发展
modules.objectives: Describe temperament types, explain Bowlby's attachment theory, distinguish secure from insecure attachment patterns, and describe the development of social referencing and basic emotions.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 4.4 — social development, attachment theory, attachment patterns, and cultural context.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 4: Infancy: Social & Emotional Development lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 4.2 — temperament dimensions and historical categories, goodness of fit, stability, and context; use it alongside assigned §4.4 on attachment.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 300-word analysis of this fictional Strange Situation pattern: Maya explores while her caregiver is present, protests at separation, seeks contact at reunion, is soothed, and resumes exploration. Include: the attachment pattern the behavior most closely resembles, evidence from separation and reunion, two alternative or contextual considerations, and the limits of one laboratory observation. Evaluation: the classification is evidence-based and clearly states that it is not a diagnosis or a basis for blaming a caregiver.

modules.title: Early Childhood: Cognitive Development
modules.objectives: Describe cognitive characteristics of the preoperational stage including symbolic thinking, egocentrism, and animism; explain theory of mind development and Vygotsky's ZPD in early education.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 5.3 — early-childhood cognition, Piaget, Vygotsky, theory of mind, and variation.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 5: Early Childhood: Cognitive Development lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 350-word analysis of this fictional false-belief task: Sam watches a ball placed in a red box and leaves; Lee moves it to a blue box; when asked where Sam will first look, a 3-year-old says 'blue' and a 5-year-old says 'red.' Include: quoted task evidence, an explanation of false-belief reasoning and theory of mind, age variation, and at least two task limitations. Evaluation: claims are tied to the transcript and do not diagnose either child.

modules.title: Early Childhood: Social-Emotional Development
modules.objectives: Describe Erikson's initiative vs. guilt stage, compare parenting styles and their research associations without treating them as deterministic, and analyze the role of play in social-emotional development.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 6.3 — family context and parenting-style dimensions, associations, and limitations.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 6: Early Childhood: Social-Emotional Development lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 5.5 — play categories, social play, cooperative play, and cultural context; use it alongside assigned §6.3 on family context and parenting dimensions.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 350-word comparison of two fictional family scenarios: Scenario A uses warm explanations, clear limits, and flexible discussion; Scenario B uses strict rules, little explanation, and low responsiveness. Include: evidence for the closest parenting-style dimensions, possible research associations stated without causation, and how child characteristics, culture, resources, stress, and context may change outcomes. Evaluation: the comparison uses scenario evidence, avoids deterministic claims, and treats the four-style framework as a simplified model.

modules.title: Language Development
modules.objectives: Trace the milestones of language development from cooing to complex syntax, evaluate nativist (Chomsky) vs. social-interactionist (Vygotsky) explanations, and explain bilingualism and critical periods.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 3.5 — early language milestones, overextension, biological preparedness, social interaction, and variation. Treat named theories as models with strengths and limits, not settled single-cause explanations.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 7: Language Development lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 5.4 — language structure, environment, and bilingual development. Its broad age-seven endpoint is not a universal cutoff: timing differs by language component, learning conditions, and outcome measured. Compare that claim with Hartshorne, Tenenbaum, and Pinker (2018), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2018.04.007, and distinguish strict critical periods from more flexible sensitive periods.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 350-word comparison of nativist and social-interactionist accounts of language acquisition using both assigned OpenStax sections and the linked Hartshorne et al. study. Include: each theory's proposed mechanism, two pieces of evidence or examples, the common cooing–babbling–first-word–two-word sequence with normal variation, implications for bilingual development, one limitation of each account, and a justified conclusion. Explain why no single birthday makes all language learning impossible. Evaluation: both theories are represented accurately, bilingualism is not treated as a deficit, critical and sensitive periods are distinguished, and the conclusion follows from cited evidence.

modules.title: Middle Childhood: School & Learning
modules.objectives: Describe Piaget's concrete operational stage abilities (conservation, classification, seriation), apply Erikson's industry vs. inferiority stage, and explain the role of school, peers, and achievement motivation.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 7.2 — concrete operations, conservation, information processing, and variation in middle childhood.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 8: Middle Childhood: School & Learning lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Lifespan Development 8.1 — apply Erikson’s industry-versus-inferiority framework to a fictional school-learning scenario.
modules.assignment: Submit: a 300-word report using this fictional conservation transcript: equal water is shown in two identical cups; one cup is poured into a taller, narrower glass; Jordan says 'the tall glass has more because the water is higher'; after the water is poured back, Jordan agrees the amounts match. Include: specific transcript evidence, conservation and reversibility concepts, one alternative task explanation, and two limits of one observation. Evaluation: the reasoning is accurately described, each claim cites the transcript, and the report avoids diagnosis.

quizQuestions.question: Piaget's theory of cognitive development is best described as:
options: Qualitative changes in thinking across cognitive stages
An innate capacity supporting the acquisition of grammar
Learning through shared cultural tools and guided participation
Gradual behavior changes chiefly through reinforcement
quizQuestions.answer: Qualitative changes in thinking across cognitive stages
quizQuestions.explanation: Piaget proposed stages characterized by qualitatively different ways of thinking. Later research questions how sharply separated and universal those stages are.

quizQuestions.question: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development emphasizes the role of:
options: Biological readiness independent of instructional support
Guided participation in tasks beyond independent ability
Repeated rewards for tasks already completed independently
Independent practice without adjusting the difficulty level
quizQuestions.answer: Guided participation in tasks beyond independent ability
quizQuestions.explanation: Vygotsky's ZPD is the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can achieve with social guidance (scaffolding).

quizQuestions.question: Which question is central to Erikson's psychosocial theory?
options: How social challenges shape development across life stages
How children revise schemas to explain new experiences
How guided participation helps children acquire cultural tools
How reinforcement changes the frequency of learned behaviors
quizQuestions.answer: How social challenges shape development across life stages
quizQuestions.explanation: Erikson described psychosocial conflicts across the lifespan and how people respond within social contexts.

quizQuestions.question: Teratogens are substances or agents that:
options: Influence prenatal development mainly through inherited genes
Can disrupt prenatal structural or functional development
Indicate the fetus’s current level of physical maturity
Provide nutrients through the developing placental circulation
quizQuestions.answer: Can disrupt prenatal structural or functional development
quizQuestions.explanation: Teratogens are exposures that can disrupt prenatal development. Effects depend on factors such as dose, timing, duration, and susceptibility; exposure is not proof of a particular outcome.

quizQuestions.question: The germinal stage of prenatal development lasts approximately:
options: Weeks 9–12 after fertilization
Weeks 13–16 after fertilization
Weeks 3–8 after fertilization
Weeks 0–2 after fertilization
quizQuestions.answer: Weeks 0–2 after fertilization
quizQuestions.explanation: The germinal stage covers fertilization through implantation of the blastocyst — approximately the first two weeks.

quizQuestions.question: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is caused by:
options: Prenatal lead exposure
Prenatal alcohol exposure
Prenatal nicotine exposure
Prenatal mercury exposure
quizQuestions.answer: Prenatal alcohol exposure
quizQuestions.explanation: FASD describes a range of effects associated with prenatal alcohol exposure. Effects and support needs vary, and a brief classroom scenario cannot establish a diagnosis.

quizQuestions.question: Why does the timing of teratogen exposure matter?
options: Earlier exposure reliably produces a milder effect than later exposure
The same dose affects each organ equally throughout pregnancy
Timing changes exposure risk mainly by changing placental nutrition
Organs and systems have different windows of greater vulnerability
quizQuestions.answer: Organs and systems have different windows of greater vulnerability
quizQuestions.explanation: The effect of an exposure can vary with dose, timing, duration, and individual susceptibility as organs develop.

quizQuestions.question: In Piaget's original sensorimotor sequence, deliberate searching for a fully hidden object is associated with which approximate substage?
options: 18–24 months
8–12 months
1–4 months
Birth to 1 month
quizQuestions.answer: 8–12 months
quizQuestions.explanation: Piaget placed deliberate search for a fully hidden object in the 8–12 month substage. Modern looking-time studies suggest some expectations about hidden objects appear earlier, so this item is specifically about Piaget’s sequence.

quizQuestions.question: The rooting reflex in newborns is best described as:
options: Closing the fingers around an object placed in the palm
Extending the arms after a sudden change in support
Turning the head toward a gentle touch on the cheek
Making stepping movements when supported in an upright position
quizQuestions.answer: Turning the head toward a gentle touch on the cheek
quizQuestions.explanation: Rooting is turning toward a touch on the cheek or near the mouth, helping an infant orient toward feeding. Grasping, Moro, and stepping responses are different reflexes.

quizQuestions.question: When responses decline to a repeated stimulus and recover to a new one, what do researchers most directly infer?
options: Memory and discrimination through stimulus responses
Motor coordination shown through reaching movements
Temperament through typical intensity of emotional reactions
Attachment security through responses to caregiver separation
quizQuestions.answer: Memory and discrimination through stimulus responses
quizQuestions.explanation: Researchers use habituation (decreased response to repeated stimuli) and dishabituation (renewed response to novelty) to infer infant cognition.

quizQuestions.question: Ainsworth's Strange Situation procedure was designed to measure:
options: Quality of motor coordination
Level of expressive language
Patterns of caregiver attachment
Level of object-classification skill
quizQuestions.answer: Patterns of caregiver attachment
quizQuestions.explanation: The Strange Situation is a structured laboratory observation of infant-caregiver attachment behavior during separation and reunion. Its classification is contextual and is not a diagnosis or a fixed prediction of later outcomes.

quizQuestions.question: Securely attached infants, when reunited with their caregiver after separation, typically:
options: Seek comfort, settle, and resume exploration
Avoid contact and focus on toys at reunion
Seek contact but resist comfort after reunion
Approach and then show contradictory, disoriented behavior
quizQuestions.answer: Seek comfort, settle, and resume exploration
quizQuestions.explanation: Secure infants use the caregiver as a safe haven — they seek comfort upon reunion, are soothed, and can resume exploration.

quizQuestions.question: Thomas and Chess's 'easy' temperament type is characterized by:
options: Slow adaptation, cautious approach, and relatively mild reactions
Irregular routines, slow adaptation, and intense negative reactions
Variable routines, intense reactions, and frequent negative mood
Regular routines, positive mood, and ready adaptation to novelty
quizQuestions.answer: Regular routines, positive mood, and ready adaptation to novelty
quizQuestions.explanation: In the classic Thomas and Chess framework, the easy category described relatively regular routines, generally positive mood, and ready adaptation. These broad historical categories do not capture every infant or determine later personality.

quizQuestions.question: Social referencing in infancy refers to:
options: Following another person’s gaze to locate a shared object
Copying an observed action to learn how an object works
Using caregiver emotion to assess an uncertain situation
Checking a mirror image to recognize one’s own reflection
quizQuestions.answer: Using caregiver emotion to assess an uncertain situation
quizQuestions.explanation: Social referencing is the infant's use of caregiver facial expressions and voice to decide how to respond to unfamiliar or uncertain situations.

quizQuestions.question: Animism, typical of the preoperational stage, refers to children's belief that:
options: A tall narrow glass holds more liquid than a short wide glass
Another observer sees an object from the child’s own viewpoint
A nonliving object can have feelings and act with intentions
A hidden object has ceased to exist when it leaves sight
quizQuestions.answer: A nonliving object can have feelings and act with intentions
quizQuestions.explanation: Preoperational animism is the attribution of life and mental states to inanimate objects (e.g., 'the rock is angry').

quizQuestions.question: Theory of mind (ToM) refers to the ability to:
options: Classify objects according to a shared physical characteristic
Represent beliefs and desires that differ from one’s own
Remember where an object was placed before it was hidden
Name an emotion by recognizing a familiar facial expression
quizQuestions.answer: Represent beliefs and desires that differ from one’s own
quizQuestions.explanation: ToM is the cognitive ability to attribute mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions) to others and understand they differ from one's own.

quizQuestions.question: A preschooler assumes everyone sees a toy exactly as they do. Which preoperational tendency does this show?
options: Egocentrism
Conservation
Object permanence
Seriation
quizQuestions.answer: Egocentrism
quizQuestions.explanation: In Piaget's account, egocentrism is difficulty taking another person's perspective.

quizQuestions.question: Which classroom example best illustrates Vygotsky's zone of proximal development?
options: A child finishes a familiar puzzle alone
A child attempts an advanced puzzle despite unhelpful prompts
A child solves a puzzle with help, but not yet alone
A child watches a partner finish a puzzle without participating
quizQuestions.answer: A child solves a puzzle with help, but not yet alone
quizQuestions.explanation: The ZPD includes tasks a learner cannot yet do independently but can complete with appropriate guidance.

quizQuestions.question: Baumrind's authoritative parenting style is characterized by:
options: High expectations with low warmth and obedience
Low expectations with low warmth and little involvement
Low expectations with high warmth and few enforced limits
High expectations with warmth and responsiveness
quizQuestions.answer: High expectations with warmth and responsiveness
quizQuestions.explanation: The authoritative style combines warmth and responsiveness with clear, developmentally appropriate expectations. Research reports average associations rather than guaranteed outcomes, and culture, child characteristics, stress, resources, and context matter.

quizQuestions.question: Erikson's initiative vs. guilt stage occurs during:
options: Adolescence, approximately ages 12–18
Infancy, approximately birth–1 year
Middle childhood, approximately ages 6–12
Early childhood, approximately ages 3–6
quizQuestions.answer: Early childhood, approximately ages 3–6
quizQuestions.explanation: Erikson's third stage occurs in the preschool years when children's expanding abilities create initiative, which guilt can suppress if overdisciplined.

quizQuestions.question: When does coordinated cooperative play with shared goals commonly become more evident?
options: Preschool years, roughly ages 4–6
Infancy, roughly birth–12 months
Early toddlerhood, roughly ages 1–2
Later childhood, roughly ages 10–12
quizQuestions.answer: Preschool years, roughly ages 4–6
quizQuestions.explanation: Coordinated cooperative play commonly becomes more evident during the preschool years. Exact timing and play patterns vary with experience, context, culture, and the activity.

quizQuestions.question: Which example best shows cooperative play?
options: Children assign roles and build a pretend store together
Children build separate stores side by side without interaction
Children watch a pretend store without taking part in it
Children share store toys without organizing a common activity
quizQuestions.answer: Children assign roles and build a pretend store together
quizQuestions.explanation: Cooperative play involves shared goals, coordinated roles, agreed rules, and reciprocal interaction, unlike parallel play in which children play near one another without organizing a common activity.

quizQuestions.question: Around what age do many infants produce recognizable first words, while normal timing varies?
options: Around 6 months of age
Around 3 months of age
Around 12 months of age
Around 24 months of age
quizQuestions.answer: Around 12 months of age
quizQuestions.explanation: Many infants produce recognizable first words near 12 months, but timing varies with language, development, opportunity, and how a word is defined; one age is not a diagnostic cutoff.

quizQuestions.question: Chomsky used the term language acquisition device (LAD) for what kind of proposal?
options: An anatomical organ identified as the specific seat of grammar
A learning process explained chiefly through reward schedules
A teaching method that uses repeated correction of sentences
A proposed innate mechanism supporting language acquisition
quizQuestions.answer: A proposed innate mechanism supporting language acquisition
quizQuestions.explanation: The LAD is a historical theoretical construct about innate language capacity, not a directly identified anatomical structure. Modern language science considers biological, cognitive, social, and cultural evidence.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement about bilingual language development is most accurate?
options: Language mixing typically signals a language disorder
Learning two languages does not inherently cause a disorder
Uneven vocabulary across languages shows that learning has stalled
Total vocabulary is best measured using only the school language
quizQuestions.answer: Learning two languages does not inherently cause a disorder
quizQuestions.explanation: Bilingual development can include uneven exposure and temporary language mixing; these patterns do not by themselves indicate a disorder.

quizQuestions.question: Conservation, mastered in the concrete operational stage, is the understanding that:
options: Objects can belong to several overlapping classification groups
Quantity stays the same despite changes in shape or arrangement
Objects can be arranged by a single measurable dimension
Events can be represented by words, drawings, or pretend actions
quizQuestions.answer: Quantity stays the same despite changes in shape or arrangement
quizQuestions.explanation: Conservation (Piaget) is the recognition that amount, number, or volume does not change when its appearance is altered.

quizQuestions.question: Erikson's industry vs. inferiority stage corresponds to:
options: Early childhood, approximately ages 3–6
Infancy, approximately birth–1 year
Middle childhood, approximately ages 6–12
Adolescence, approximately ages 12–18
quizQuestions.answer: Middle childhood, approximately ages 6–12
quizQuestions.explanation: Erikson's fourth stage occurs during the school years; children develop competence (industry) through mastery of skills or feel inferior when they fail.

quizQuestions.question: Seriation in the concrete operational stage refers to the ability to:
options: Order objects along a dimension such as length
Sort objects into groups by shared characteristics
Mentally undo an action to restore its earlier state
Use a familiar object to represent something else
quizQuestions.answer: Order objects along a dimension such as length
quizQuestions.explanation: Seriation is the ability to mentally arrange a set of objects in order along a quantitative dimension — mastered in concrete operations.

quizQuestions.question: A child gains confidence by mastering school tasks and receiving constructive feedback. Which Erikson stage does this illustrate?
options: Identity vs. role confusion
Trust vs. mistrust
Generativity vs. stagnation
Industry vs. inferiority
quizQuestions.answer: Industry vs. inferiority
quizQuestions.explanation: During middle childhood, successful effort and recognition can support a sense of competence or industry.

questions.question: Piaget's concept of assimilation refers to:
options: Interpreting new information through an existing schema
Advancing from one cognitive stage to the next
Resolving cognitive conflict through equilibration
Altering an existing schema to explain a new experience
questions.answer: Interpreting new information through an existing schema
questions.explanation: Assimilation is the process of interpreting new experiences through an existing schema without changing the schema.

questions.question: Which statement about alcohol exposure during pregnancy is safest and most accurate?
options: Small amounts of wine are established as safe after early pregnancy
Avoiding intoxication establishes a safe exposure level in pregnancy
No safe amount or timing is established; avoiding alcohol is advised
Exposure matters chiefly during the weeks when organs first form
questions.answer: No safe amount or timing is established; avoiding alcohol is advised
questions.explanation: Alcohol can affect development throughout pregnancy, and no amount or timing has been established as safe.

questions.question: Object permanence develops during Piaget's:
options: Preoperational stage
Sensorimotor stage
Formal operational stage
Concrete operational stage
questions.answer: Sensorimotor stage
questions.explanation: Object permanence develops during the sensorimotor period. Searching behavior often appears in the latter half of the first year, while other research methods can detect some expectations earlier.

questions.question: Which caregiving context most directly illustrates a caregiver becoming both a potential source of comfort and a source of fear?
options: Frightening or frightened caregiving and severe caregiving disruption
Consistently sensitive responses to an infant’s bids for comfort
Repeated rebuffing of contact without frightened caregiver behavior
Inconsistent comfort without frightening or disoriented interactions
questions.answer: Frightening or frightened caregiving and severe caregiving disruption
questions.explanation: Frightening or frightened caregiving can create an approach-avoidance conflict when the caregiver is both a potential source of comfort and a source of fear. Research associations do not prove a cause in a particular family, and a single observation cannot establish a diagnosis.

questions.question: By what age do most children pass a standard verbal false-belief task?
options: 18 months
2 years
8 years
4–5 years
questions.answer: 4–5 years
questions.explanation: Most children pass standard verbal false-belief tasks around ages 4–5, but performance depends on language, task demands, culture, and experience; theory of mind is broader than one task.

questions.question: In many studies, which pattern is associated with authoritative parenting?
options: Low warmth and strict obedience are linked to stronger peer competence
Warmth with few enforced limits reliably predicts stronger self-regulation
Warmth and limits have the same effects regardless of culture or resources
Warmth and clear limits are associated with stronger average outcomes
questions.answer: Warmth and clear limits are associated with stronger average outcomes
questions.explanation: Many studies report positive average associations, but the framework is simplified and outcomes also reflect culture, child characteristics, resources, stress, and other contexts.

questions.question: Overextension in early language development refers to:
options: Applying a word to a broader category than intended
Applying a regular grammar rule to an irregular word
Applying a word to a narrower category than intended
Creating a new word for an unfamiliar object
questions.answer: Applying a word to a broader category than intended
questions.explanation: Overextension is applying a word too broadly — calling all men 'daddy' or all round objects 'ball.'

questions.question: Conservation of liquid quantity is mastered during Piaget's:
options: Preoperational stage
Concrete operational stage
Formal operational stage
Sensorimotor stage
questions.answer: Concrete operational stage
questions.explanation: Conservation tasks are typically mastered during the concrete operational stage.

questions.question: A caregiver hides a toy, and an infant searches for it. Which concept does this behavior demonstrate?
options: Overextension
Animism
Seriation
Object permanence
questions.answer: Object permanence
questions.explanation: Searching for a hidden object indicates understanding that it continues to exist when out of sight.

questions.question: Which observation best illustrates social referencing?
options: An infant follows a caregiver’s gaze to locate a toy on a shelf
An infant copies a caregiver’s action to open an unfamiliar box
An infant checks a caregiver’s emotion before trying a new toy
An infant points toward a new toy to share interest with a caregiver
questions.answer: An infant checks a caregiver’s emotion before trying a new toy
questions.explanation: Social referencing uses another person's emotional cues to guide a response to an uncertain situation.

questions.question: A preschooler says, 'The moon wants to keep us company, so it follows our car.' Which preoperational concept best fits?
options: Formal operations
Conservation
Animism
Seriation
questions.answer: Animism
questions.explanation: The child attributes intention and purpose to a nonliving object. That added evidence distinguishes animism from merely noticing apparent motion.

questions.question: Which caregiver response best reflects an authoritative style?
options: Let the child decide the limit to prevent further conflict
Explain a clear limit and listen to the child’s perspective
Enforce the limit without discussing the child’s concerns
Postpone the limit and give reassurance to stop the distress
questions.answer: Explain a clear limit and listen to the child’s perspective
questions.explanation: Authoritative parenting combines warmth and responsiveness with clear, developmentally appropriate expectations.

questions.question: A child calls every four-legged animal 'dog.' Which language pattern is this?
options: Underextension
Overextension
Overregularization
Telegraphic speech
questions.answer: Overextension
questions.explanation: Overextension applies a familiar word to a category broader than its conventional meaning.

questions.question: Which ability is characteristic of concrete operational thinking?
options: Judging quantity mainly from the height of a container
Attributing intentions to objects that appear to move
Conserving quantity despite changes in visible arrangement
Solving purely hypothetical problems without concrete examples
questions.answer: Conserving quantity despite changes in visible arrangement
questions.explanation: Concrete operational thinkers can apply logical rules such as conservation to tangible situations.

questions.question: Vygotsky's emphasis on the ZPD has the most direct implications for:
options: Providing guidance just beyond independent ability
Assigning tasks according to biological age alone
Repeating familiar tasks before introducing new ones
Rewarding performance without adjusting instructional support
questions.answer: Providing guidance just beyond independent ability
questions.explanation: The ZPD implies that optimal instruction targets skills slightly above current ability, with expert guidance (scaffolding) to support acquisition.

questions.question: Accommodation in Piaget's theory involves:
options: Changing a schema to explain new information
Repeating a learned response after receiving reinforcement
Using an existing schema for new information
Copying a modeled action to obtain a similar outcome
questions.answer: Changing a schema to explain new information
questions.explanation: Accommodation changes schemas; assimilation fits new experiences into schemas already in place.

questions.question: Why is the embryonic stage especially vulnerable to teratogens that cause major structural malformations?
options: Prenatal exposures accumulate only during this stage
Small fetal size prevents dilution of any exposure
The nervous system is already fully mature at this stage
Major organs are rapidly forming during this stage
questions.answer: Major organs are rapidly forming during this stage
questions.explanation: Organogenesis occurs mainly in weeks 3–8, creating high vulnerability to major structural malformations; susceptibility to other effects varies by system, timing, dose, and context.

questions.question: Which reflex is shown when a newborn responds to a sudden sensation by extending the arms and then drawing them inward?
options: Rooting reflex
Moro reflex
Babinski reflex
Stepping reflex
questions.answer: Moro reflex
questions.explanation: The Moro or startle reflex includes arm extension followed by flexion after a sudden stimulus.

questions.question: Which caregiver behavior is commonly associated with secure attachment, while remaining only one part of a larger developmental context?
options: Responding sensitively to the infant’s changing signals
Redirecting contact bids toward independent play each time
Delaying comfort mainly to teach the infant self-reliance
Using a fixed response without attending to the infant’s cues
questions.answer: Responding sensitively to the infant’s changing signals
questions.explanation: Caregiver sensitivity has a reliable but not deterministic association with attachment security; temperament, culture, caregiving networks, stress, and measurement context also matter.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects current developmental science?
options: Age norms identify the same developmental sequence for each child
Stage labels provide enough evidence to predict adult outcomes
Age trends coexist with individual and contextual variation
One carefully observed milestone can establish a developmental diagnosis
questions.answer: Age trends coexist with individual and contextual variation
questions.explanation: Developmental theories organize common patterns, while evidence also shows variation and context. Conclusions should use repeated, appropriate evidence rather than one observation or deterministic stage labels.

questions.question: Which parenting style is defined by low responsiveness and low demandingness?
questions.answer: Uninvolved (neglectful)
questions.explanation: In the four-style framework, uninvolved parenting is characterized by low responsiveness and low demandingness; the label describes a pattern and does not by itself prove a child's outcome.

questions.question: A child repeatedly calls cats, cows, and horses 'doggy.' Which language pattern does this best demonstrate?
options: Telegraphic speech
Overregularization
Underextension
Overextension
questions.answer: Overextension
questions.explanation: Repeatedly applying 'doggy' to several different four-legged-animal categories is overextension rather than a single possible misidentification.

questions.question: A child understands that the amount of water stays the same after it is poured into a taller glass. Which concept is demonstrated?
options: Conservation
Animism
Object permanence
Overextension
questions.answer: Conservation
questions.explanation: Conservation is understanding that quantity remains constant despite a change in appearance.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly orders early language milestones?
options: Babbling, complex syntax, cooing, first words
Two-word combinations, babbling, cooing, first words
Cooing, babbling, first words, two-word combinations
First words, cooing, two-word combinations, babbling
questions.answer: Cooing, babbling, first words, two-word combinations
questions.explanation: Although timing varies, this sequence reflects a common progression in early language development.

questions.question: Which example best shows scaffolding?
options: An adult repeats identical instructions despite changes in the child’s skill
An adult finishes a task so the child can observe the correct result
An adult adjusts prompts and fades support as the child gains skill
An adult gives a fixed reward without changing support for the task
questions.answer: An adult adjusts prompts and fades support as the child gains skill
questions.explanation: Scaffolding provides adjustable support within the learner's zone of proximal development.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes critical and sensitive periods?
options: Critical refers to faster physical growth; sensitive refers to emotional growth
Critical implies required timing; sensitive implies heightened responsiveness
Critical refers to school-taught skills; sensitive refers to home-taught skills
Critical implies gradual change; sensitive implies a fixed developmental cutoff
questions.answer: Critical implies required timing; sensitive implies heightened responsiveness
questions.explanation: A critical period is a relatively restricted window when particular input is required for typical development of a function. A sensitive period offers heightened responsiveness with more flexibility. Neither term should be used as a blanket claim that later learning is impossible.

questions.question: Which behavior best demonstrates theory of mind?
options: Tracking an object’s path and locating it after it leaves sight
Ordering objects by size and explaining how they were sorted
Predicting a search from someone else’s mistaken belief
Recognizing emotion in a familiar person’s face
questions.answer: Predicting a search from someone else’s mistaken belief
questions.explanation: False-belief reasoning requires representing another person's mental state as different from reality and from one's own knowledge.

questions.question: Which statement about attachment patterns is most accurate?
options: They describe contextual relationship behavior, not a standalone diagnosis
They describe stable infant temperament across different relationships
They predict adult relationship outcomes from one infant observation
They identify caregiving quality without considering culture or conditions
questions.answer: They describe contextual relationship behavior, not a standalone diagnosis
questions.explanation: Attachment classifications summarize behavior in a specific assessment context; development reflects many relationships and conditions.

questions.question: Which example best shows seriation?
options: Sorting sticks into separate groups by their color
Arranging sticks from shortest to longest in order
Recognizing that hidden sticks continue to exist
Counting sticks again after their spacing changes
questions.answer: Arranging sticks from shortest to longest in order
questions.explanation: Seriation is the ability to order objects along a measurable dimension such as length, weight, or number, a skill associated with concrete operational reasoning.

questions.question: Which statement best compares temperament and parenting?
options: Temperament chiefly records the caregiving a child has already received
Early behavioral tendencies interact with caregiving and context over time
Parenting styles and temperament describe the same individual differences
Temperament fixes later behavior largely independently of relationships
questions.answer: Early behavioral tendencies interact with caregiving and context over time
questions.explanation: Development emerges through interaction among individual characteristics, relationships, and broader contexts.

questions.question: Which is one major evidence-based criticism of Piaget's stage account?
options: It treated social relationships as the primary cause of cognitive change
It explained cognitive changes chiefly through rewards and punishments
Some original tasks underestimated abilities detected with other methods
It described development as gradual accumulation without qualitative shifts
questions.answer: Some original tasks underestimated abilities detected with other methods
questions.explanation: Later studies using looking-time, simplified tasks, and other methods found some abilities earlier than Piaget’s original tasks suggested; researchers also debate how discrete and universal the stages are.

questions.question: The strange situation experiment by Ainsworth involved observing infants in response to:
options: Responses to questions about motives in a moral dilemma
Responses to liquid poured between differently shaped cups
Responses to new toys and unfamiliar problem-solving tasks
Responses to caregiver separations, reunions, and a stranger
questions.answer: Responses to caregiver separations, reunions, and a stranger
questions.explanation: Ainsworth's Strange Situation assesses attachment behavior during separations, reunions, and stranger episodes.

questions.question: In Erikson’s account of middle childhood, a child masters school tasks with useful feedback. Which psychosocial strength can grow?
options: Industry or competence
Identity or self-definition
Autonomy or self-direction
Initiative or purposeful action
questions.answer: Industry or competence
questions.explanation: Erikson linked middle childhood and mastery of school tasks with industry or competence. Autonomy and initiative are associated with earlier psychosocial conflicts, while identity is especially associated with adolescence.

questions.question: A baby turns toward a gentle touch on the cheek and opens the mouth. Which reflex is this?
options: Palmar grasp reflex
Rooting reflex
Babinski reflex
Moro reflex
questions.answer: Rooting reflex
questions.explanation: The rooting reflex helps a newborn orient toward a possible feeding source.

questions.question: Why should one developmental observation be interpreted cautiously?
options: Standard tasks eliminate language and culture effects
A typical age range provides a firm cutoff for each individual child
A single observation reveals a stable ability regardless of setting
Behavior varies with context, task, and the child’s state
questions.answer: Behavior varies with context, task, and the child’s state
questions.explanation: Developmental conclusions should use repeated evidence and context rather than treating one observation as deterministic.
